title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency with R
text:
In this post, I use R to explore the relationship between vehicle characteristics and fuel efficiency using the mtcars dataset.
Data: mtcars, included with R in the datasets package.
The dataset contains fuel consumption and automobile design characteristics for 32 cars.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency with R
text:
Inspect the data

head(mtcars)

                   mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
Mazda RX4         21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
Datsun 710        22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6  258 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
Hornet Sportabout 18.7   8  360 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2
Valiant           18.1   6  225 105 2.76 3.460 20.22  1  0    3    1


The dataset includes variables such as miles per gallon (mpg), vehicle weight (wt), horsepower (hp), and number of cylinders (cyl).

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency with R
text:
Summarize fuel efficiency

summary(mtcars$mpg)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  10.40   15.43   19.20   20.09   22.80   33.90 


The summary shows considerable variation in fuel efficiency across the 32 vehicles.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency with R
section: Compare fuel efficiency by cylinder count
text:
Compare fuel efficiency by cylinder count

aggregate(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars, FUN = mean)

  cyl      mpg
1   4 26.66364
2   6 19.74286
3   8 15.10000


Cars with fewer cylinders have higher average fuel efficiency in this dataset.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency with R
text:
Examine weight and fuel efficiency

plot(
  mtcars$wt,
  mtcars$mpg,
  xlab = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
  ylab = "Miles per gallon",
  main = "Vehicle Weight and Fuel Efficiency"
)

abline(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars))







Figure 1: Relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency.





The plot shows a negative relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency. Heavier vehicles generally have lower miles per gallon.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency with R
text:
Conclusion
This analysis shows that vehicle characteristics are related to fuel efficiency. In this dataset, heavier cars and cars with more cylinders tend to have lower fuel efficiency.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
My first weeks in MDS at UBC.


My first few weeks in the Master of Data Science program have been exciting and intense. Orientation gave me a chance to meet my classmates and learn more about how the program is structured. Once classes started, I quickly realized how fast-paced the program is and how much material we cover in a short period of time.
One thing that surprised me was how quickly we started working with different tools and programming languages. I have already been using Python, R, Git, GitHub, the terminal, and Quarto. Some of these were unfamiliar to me at the beginning, but I am becoming more comfortable with them through practice.
Now that I am a couple of weeks into the program, I feel much more settled. There is still a lot to learn, but I am starting to understand the workflow and feel more confident solving problems on my own. I am looking forward to seeing how much I improve over the rest of the program.

title: Using R and Python Together
text: This post demonstrates how R and Python can work together in one Quarto document using the reticulate package. I create an object in R, use it in Python, and then pass the Python result back to R.

title: Using R and Python Together
text: This post demonstrates how R and Python can work together in one Quarto document using the reticulate package. I create an object in R, use it in Python, and then pass the Python result back to R.

title: Using R and Python Together
text:
Create an object in R

library(reticulate)

numbers <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)
numbers

[1] 10 20 30 40 50


The R object numbers contains five numeric values.

title: Using R and Python Together
section: Use the R object in Python
text:
Use the R object in Python

numbers_from_r = list(r.numbers)

python_mean = sum(numbers_from_r) / len(numbers_from_r)

python_mean

30.0


Python accesses the object created in R and calculates its mean.

title: Using R and Python Together
section: Use the Python result in R
text:
Use the Python result in R

mean_from_python <- py$python_mean
mean_from_python

[1] 30


The value calculated in Python is now available in R.

title: Using R and Python Together
text:
Verify the result

mean(numbers)

[1] 30


Both calculations produce the same mean. This demonstrates that an object can be passed from R to Python and that a result computed in Python can then be used in R within the same Quarto document.

Introduction
In this post, I use Python to explore relationships between flower measurements in the Iris dataset.
Data: Iris dataset, accessed through scikit-learn.
The dataset contains measurements of sepal and petal dimensions for three iris species.

title: Jaclyn Liu

Load the data

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
import pandas as pd

The dataset contains four numerical flower measurements and a target variable representing species.

title: Jaclyn Liu
text:
Calculate mean measurements by species

df["species"] = df["target"].map(
    dict(enumerate(iris.target_names))
)

species_means = df.groupby("species")[
    ["sepal length (cm)", "petal length (cm)"]
].mean()

species_means

The species differ substantially in their average petal lengths. Setosa has much shorter petals than versicolor and virginica.

title: Jaclyn Liu
text:
Visualize petal length and width

for species in df["species"].unique():
    subset = df[df["species"] == species]
    plt.scatter(
        subset["petal length (cm)"],
        subset["petal width (cm)"],
        label=species
    )

plt.xlabel("Petal length (cm)")
plt.ylabel("Petal width (cm)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Petal length and petal width for the three Iris species.





The figure shows a strong positive relationship between petal length and petal width. Setosa is clearly separated from the other two species, while versicolor and virginica overlap somewhat.

title: Jaclyn Liu
text:
Conclusion
This analysis shows that Iris species differ noticeably in their flower measurements. Petal length and width are particularly useful for distinguishing the species.
